about: How `-x` tokens bind. A short flag taking a value accepts it attached, attached after `=`, or as the following word. Several value-less shorts may be bundled in one token.

vectors.doc: A short alias sets the flag it belongs to, recorded under the flag's name.
`-j 8` binds the following word.
`-j8` binds the rest of the token. mise relies on this for `-C/tmp` and `-Edev`.
An attached value keeps every character after the flag letter, including leading slashes and equals-free punctuation.
`-j=8` binds `8`, not `=8`. A single leading `=` is a separator, matching the long form.
Only one `=` is a separator, so `-j==8` binds `=8`. A value that begins with `=` is reachable, rather than being eaten by a second round of separator-stripping.
`-j=` binds the empty string, matching `--jobs=`. Both attached forms can express present-but-empty.
An empty token is not flag-like, so it is an ordinary detached value here too.
`-f -` binds `-`, the conventional name for stdin. A lone dash is not flag-like, so the rule refusing flag-like detached values does not reach it — without that, `sort -o -` could not be written.
A value-taking short at the end of the command line is an error.
Value-less shorts may share a token: `-ab` sets both.
A bundle may end with a value-taking short, which then consumes the remainder of the token.
A token containing an unrecognized letter is not a bundle at all, so none of its letters are applied — `-az` does not set `-a`. Here it becomes a word, and there is no argument to hold it.

The same rejection, seen from the side that matters: with an argument free to take the token, `-a` must still be unset. A token containing an unrecognized letter was never a bundle, so none of its letters apply — the previous vector cannot show this, because both readings produce the same error.

`=` is a separator only for a short that takes a value. After one that does not, it is just an unrecognized letter, so `-f=yes` is not a bundle and `-f` is not set — the whole token becomes a word, as `-az` does.
A `count` flag records how many times it appeared, so `-vvv` is three.
The same count reached through separate tokens gives the same result.
A counting short keeps counting inside a bundle, so `-avv` is `-a` once and `-v` twice.
A lone `-` is a value, conventionally meaning stdin, not a flag.
An unrecognized short flag is a word too, for the same reason as the long form.
Refusing unknown flags, an unrecognized letter fails the whole token rather than applying the letters before it — a partly-applied bundle would be worse than a rejected one.
`-1x` is not a number, so it is a flag-shaped token that names nothing — a CLI refusing unknown flags hears about it rather than having it slip through as a value.

`-1e5` is a number, so it is a value even where unknown flags are refused. The two parsers disagreed about this when one used a float parse and the other a hand-written scanner, which is why the edges are pinned here.
A signed exponent on a fraction is still a number.
`-inf` parses as a float but is not treated as one: a token like that is far likelier to be a misspelled flag than a number somebody meant to pass, so a CLI refusing unknown flags hears about it.
An exponent needs digits of its own, so `-1e` names nothing.
The short form of `allow_hyphen_values`: `-a -destroy` binds `-destroy` rather than reading `-d` as a different short and attaching `estroy`.
A short's attached form still binds under `require_equals`: `-i9229` never needed a following word.
`-i=9229` is attached too: the `=` is a separator, not a following word.
`-i 9229` is the following word, so `require_equals` refuses it the same way `--inspect 9229` is refused.
The short form of `default_missing`: `-c` with no following word binds the missing default.
A short's attached form still binds: `-cnever` is `never`.
`-c -v` colours with the missing default and still sets verbose.
